translations.text: Discourse of our holy and blessed father Gregory of Nyssa on virginity and the divine way of life. Bless us, O Lord!
The purpose of this our discourse, O beloved, is this: to instill in the hearts of its readers a desire for the virtuous life.

And since in the way of life of the world, as the holy apostle says, there are many tumults and distractions, for this reason in this our book we have placed virginity first, as the door and entrance to the honorable life and the divine way of life. For it is hardly possible for those who are bound by the bonds of the world to devote themselves in stillness to that divine life,

but for those who have withdrawn from this life full of turmoil it is very easy to remain "free of care" and "steadfast" in the lofty contemplations of the mind, once they stand apart from the turmoils of the world.
And since teaching given so plainly is not very effective for persuasion, and no one can bend a person toward any undertaking by simple speech,

unless he first praises and shows to be honorable the undertaking to which he wishes to bring the one he is teaching, for this reason this our discourse begins first with the praise of virginity and so proceeds to teaching;

and since the good is shown more clearly when the hardship of its opposite has been revealed, for this reason we have also mentioned the hardship of that worldly life, and afterward introduced a depiction of the virtuous life, and also shown that one who is caught up in the cares of the world cannot attain it.
And since those who have gone out from the world must drive out bodily desire entirely, for this reason, in the proper place, we have fittingly inquired what that true object of desire is
for the sake of which the power of desire was given to our nature by the Creator.
And once we had shown this as far as we were able, there next followed the inquiry as to what means we might find for attaining that true good.
And true virginity was found, separated from all the defilements of sin,
to be good and effective as such a means; and our discourse, even though it may turn aside now to one thing and now to another, strives in every way for the praise of virginity.
But our discourse has passed over the individual practices discovered by those who pursue this honorable life, for it was fleeing excess;

it has only mentioned the roots of the commandments and given teaching about them, and it has also brought this in so that no one should neglect any of the good things, while also fleeing from excess. And since when a person sees certain people

who have become greatly distinguished in some undertaking, he grows eager to take up that undertaking, for this reason we have rightly mentioned the saints who were distinguished in celibacy. And since ancient examples of virtue do not make a person as eager as those recently set,
for this reason we have fittingly mentioned, in the concluding part of the discourse, the virtue of the bishop and our father, as the only one capable of teaching such things.
But this mention has been made not by name, but through the deeds that show of whom our discourse speaks,
so that those who read our discourse after our time may not have their minds looking toward what is past, but may only understand how such a life ought properly to be lived in its various forms,

and may take such people as guides to virtue, so that they may either find what they seek, or at least not be ignorant of what is proper. As for you, when you read, you will find the substance of these words to be as follows:
First, that virginity is above all praise;
and next, that virginity is proper to the holy and bodiless nature;
and after this will be found a mention of the hardship that marriage entails, and that the speaker of these words also once fell into those bonds;
and next, that all the afflictions of this life have their beginning from marriage, and what kind of person is truly separated from the world;
and after this you will find that freedom of the soul from passion must go before purity of the body;
and next you will read that Elijah and John acquired this good way of life;
and again, that neither is marriage evil;
and next, that a person whose soul is scattered among many affairs will hardly acquire that desired life;
and that it is difficult in every matter to change a habit;
and after this you will find what true desire is;
and by what means one may find that true good;
and that whoever has purified himself will see that divine beauty within himself;
and that the beginning of care for oneself is separation from marriage;
and that virginity is superior to the tyranny of death;
and that true virginity is seen in every activity;
and that if anyone goes even a little beyond the bounds of virtue, he is liable to judgment;
and that whoever is lacking in even one virtue is imperfect with respect to the good;
and that all the powers of the soul must look toward virtue;
after this you will find a mention of Miriam, the sister of Aaron, that she began this way of life;
and next, that it is impossible for the soul to be a slave to bodily desires and also to have that divine joy;
and that whoever wishes to live a good life must become a stranger to every bodily desire;
and that even ascetic struggle beyond measure is not good, for both complete bodily indulgence and immoderate labor oppose the soul;
and next you will find this: that whoever would learn this life well must learn it from one who has succeeded in it.
Discourse of our holy father Gregory of Nyssa. Chapter [?]. The honourable practice of virginity, which is desired by all who understand the true good,

but is found only among those whose good intention the grace of God supports in their desire for this virtue, has in itself its fitting praise from the name that is given to it. For it is called incorruption, which points to its great purity. Therefore the name alone is enough to show how far the honour of this great grace surpasses others. For the kinds of virtue are many and countless, and this one alone is honoured with the name of incorruption.
If praise of this great gift of God in words of eulogy is needed at all, the holy apostle Paul is enough to praise it,
who with a few words covered every word of encomium, for he gave the name "holy and blameless" to those adorned by this grace.
For if the practice of virginity is this, that it makes the one who acquires it "holy and blameless," these names are, by nature and in truth, the glorifying titles of God the Creator.

For when we glorify him, we call him "holy and blameless." And since virginity bestows the names that are given to God on the people who practice it, what higher praise of it could there be than this, that it makes those who share in its mysteries like God, so that they may become partakers of the glory of the only truly holy and blameless and incorruptible God,
having been made his own and proper through holiness and incorruption? But those who compose long speeches to extol virginity and suppose

that by their words they have added something to its glory, these, as I think, oppose their own intention and do not realize that by those words of encomium, with which they suppose that they are exalting virginity, they rather make it suspect.

for things that have glory by their very nature carry their praise in themselves and need no help from words. In the same way, the height of the sky and the brightness of the sun need no words to show them. They show their own height and brightness.
But things that are lowly by nature need to have their lowliness raised a little by a word of encomium. And for this reason a matter exalted by people's words often becomes suspect to many.
But the true and worthy praise of virginity is this: that a person should determine that this virtue is above the rule of praise, and should glorify purity by deed rather than by word.
But whoever hastens to extol and praise it by word is like a man who supposes that a drop of his own sweat is adequate to increase the great depths of the sea;
so it is with one who supposes that by his own word he is able to glorify such a grace any further: either he is ignorant of his own power, or he does not know what he is praising.

Chapter 1. For we need great knowledge in order to understand the surpassing excellence of this grace, which is perceived together with the incorruptible Father, who without passion begot the beginningless Son and Word,
and it is seen together with the only-begotten Son and God, the giver of incorruption, for it shone forth together with his pure and passionless birth,
and likewise, in the same way, it appears together with the incorruption and natural holiness of the Holy Spirit.
For whenever one says "pure" and "incorruptible," one is speaking under another name of the very nature of virginity, which, as I said,

is seen together with the Holy Trinity and, through impassibility, shares the way of life of all the natures above. And it dwells with those supreme powers: it is neither separated from any of the holy ones nor joined to any of the adversaries.
For all who by nature and in mind look toward virtue and are lovers of it are all adorned with that purity of incorruption.
And all who are inclined to the opposing side are such because of their fall from purity. What power of words, then, could be found equal to such a grace?
Or how should we not be afraid that our words might harm its loftiness, by giving those who hear our words an idea of it that falls short of its own natural glory? 2.
And therefore it is good for us to refrain from words of eulogy about it, since our speech cannot rise to its height. But, as far as we are able,

let us remember this good virtue and always keep it on our tongue and in our heart. It properly belongs to the bodiless nature, but through God's love for humankind it has been granted to us as well, who live a life bound up with flesh and blood,
so that it might extend this virtue of virginity like a hand to human nature, fallen through its passionate mind, and raise it up and make it look once again toward the glory of heaven. For I think
that this is why the very fountain of incorruption, our Lord Jesus Christ, did not enter the world through marriage:
to show by his own incarnation this great mystery, that virginity and purity bring about the coming of God and his dwelling among us,
which it is impossible to truly gain in any other way, except that a person make himself entirely a stranger to the passions of the flesh.
For what happened bodily in the incorrupt Mary, since "the fullness of Christ God" shone forth from her virginity, this same thing happens in every soul that has acquired true virginity.
For the Lord's coming no longer takes place bodily, but he dwells spiritually in the soul, together with his Father, as he himself says in the Gospel. 3.
And since such is the power of virginity,

that it abides even in the heavens with the Father of spirits, and brings about the salvation of human beings, and through itself brings God to share in human life, and through itself leads human beings to the desire of heavenly things

And since it becomes a kind of bond of the union of human beings with God, and by its mediation brings into unity those who are by nature so far removed from one another, what power of words could be found to rise to the height of its wonders?

But since it is not good that we should be altogether like those who are senseless and speechless, so that one of two things might not be said of us: either that the good things of virginity are unknown to us,
or that we are unfeeling and unmoved to desire the true good, for this reason let us say some small thing about it.
But let no one seek from us philosophical speeches composed with intricate skill, for perhaps even if we wished it, we could not accomplish such a thing, we who are untaught in such speech.
Yet even if we had the ability, we would not abandon speaking for the benefit of all and strive to please a certain few.
For it befits a wise man not to do the sort of thing for which others may praise him, but that by which he may benefit both himself and others.
Chapter

and would that it were possible for me too to profit from such zeal, so that I might have carried out this labour with greater zeal, if, as Scripture says, I were labouring at this discourse "in hope," so that I too might receive the fruit of my "ploughing and sowing."

But as it is, knowing and understanding the good things of virginity is of no use at all to me. It is like the grain to an ox that goes round the threshing floor with a muzzle on, or like water flowing below a cliff to a thirsty man who cannot reach it.
But blessed are those in whose power lies the choice of the better, and for whom their former life has not become a dividing wall.

As for us, it is as though by some deep chasm lying between us that we are separated from the glory of virginity, to which it is no longer possible for anyone to return who has once entered upon secular life.
For this reason we are only spectators of the good of others and witnesses of the blessedness of others, and even if we understand something and speak about virginity,
we are like cooks and servants who prepare delicious foods for their rich masters and do not themselves get a taste.
And it would have been a blessed thing if it were not so, and if we had not come to know this good only after falling into the snare.
But now, just as those who see their own poverty beside the wealth of others
are pained in mind all the more, so too, the more we understand the good of virginity, the more pitiable we find the other life, seeing what great and how many good things it lacks.
I do not speak only of the good things that in the age to come are given to those who have lived virtuously,

but also of how many advantages virginity has in this life. For if anyone wishes to compare the good of this worldly life with virginity and the monastic life, he will find as great a difference as there is between earth and heaven. It is good for us to understand the truth of this statement by looking at the facts.
But from what point should one begin speaking, so as to set forth worthily the circumstances of this grievous and wretched life?
Or how could anyone expose the evils of this world, which all people know from experience? And I do not know how the world has contrived, by means of its own snares, against those who know them.
And do people willfully refuse to understand what they are living in?! For look at its evils:
Let us say that there is a rich man, of noble parents, joined to a wife who is likewise noble, and that he is in the flower of youth,
that they have great love for each other, and that they have as much glory and power as they wish.
But see how, along with all these good things, grief is joined to them even here. I will leave aside the envy of others,
[?] which is in such a thing, and the conflicts [?] that come about through others, as is the custom and practice of the world. I will leave all this aside and say,
unless envy and strife come upon them from others — which you would not fail to know
whether such a person has been found anywhere who had wealth and high rank and had no enemies or envious rivals at all.
But let us say that their life is free from all such things, and let us see whether either of them can live in joy.
And if you say, "What then could there be to distress such a person?", first understand this:
that when they look upon the graves of their fathers and know the corruptibility of human nature, they have grief that is inseparable from their life,
if one has even a little understanding and knows human nature.

And as for the other evils of the world, what more can anyone say? If anyone could understand them properly, would he ever stay in it, and not flee from it at a run and enter the life of ascetic struggle? For he would see that the affairs of this world are laughable,
mixed with tears, and grief joined with joy,

and death made ready alongside every affair and coming mercilessly upon every age. And the one who today is beautiful and living in delight is tomorrow in the grave, loathsome and stinking and reduced to nothing, and neither trace nor memory of his fine state is to be seen.
If a person reflects on this and things like it, how could he believe the lie of this world's good things?
and would he not, as with the fancies of a dream,
look on this world and its affairs as things truly foreign to him?
For none of the good things of this world is true; rather, it is one thing and appears to us as another,

and with the hope of good it deceives those who love it, and it hides itself in the crevices of delight and brief joy, until at the time of change its lie is revealed: how it was one thing and appeared as another and deceived people in vain.
What joy, then, could come to the heart of one who reflects on all this?
When could the heart of one who understands this well and recognizes the nature of this world's affairs become glad over this transient life? 8.

And if you wish to learn the hardship of this world, hear what those who are experienced in the matter by actual practice say: how they call blessed those who have remained in virginity from the beginning, and again those who have left it and departed from it.
For virginity and true monastic life are free from all these evils. It knows no mourning over orphanhood, nor lamentation over widowhood, but is forever united with that incorruptible Bridegroom,
forever rejoices over the offspring of godliness, and forever sees that house which is truly its own adorned with every good thing,
For in such a one dwells the King of all. For this person death brings no separation; rather, it brings union with the true Bridegroom whom the soul longs for,
for when she "departs," then she "is united with Christ," as the Apostle says.

But what shall we say about the other ways of life in this world? For concerning those who are wealthy and free of hardship we have said this little: that it is impossible for them to be without grief.

But what shall we say about the others, who were in poverty and hardship and in those countless trials of the world that are joined to human life? From all of these a person who cares only for his own soul either escapes, or,
if they come upon him, he easily endures those trials, since his mind is gathered into himself alone and is not scattered in many directions by cares.

But the one who is turned to the care of worldly affairs does not even have leisure to sigh over his own evils; rather, the mind of the married person is scattered toward wife and children and those other countless cares.
And why should we say much? For if the rich and the great are not spared evil and grief and hardship, what need is there to speak about the afflicted and the poor?!
Or even if we should wish to, where could words be found adequate to express those evils,
for the rich and the great are distressed by the expectation or the coming of death, but the poor and the afflicted by its delay.
And the life of the rich and that of the poor are very far from one another, yet the grief and hardship of both are countless and indescribable.
Thus on every side marriage is a snare and a bringer of hardships, for if children are born, they are a trial, and if they are not born, a grief.

And again, if they live, they are a burden, and if they die, a cause of mourning. And one man has many children and does not even have food with which to feed himself, while another, with his many possessions acquired through hardship and sin, does not even have offspring as an heir.

And to each of these two, the other's trial seems good: the destitute man with many children longs for childlessness, while the childless rich man considers that poor man with many children to be blessed.

And again, one man's beloved child dies, and another's lives on, disobedient and wicked. And both are pitiable: the one mourns the death of his beloved child, and the other the hardships caused by that wicked living one.
And what shall I say of the wars and the enmities of one against another, and of the kinds of trials and sufferings in which these things end?
For who could count them all one by one? But you, if you wish to know how full of evil the life of the world is,
if you believe the sayings of the ancients, read them,
in which you found killings of children, slayings of fathers and mothers, murders of brothers, lawless unions, and every kind of disturbance and corruption of nature,
all of which begin their narrative from marriage and bring their story to its end through such calamities.
But if you do not believe those ancient accounts, look at these present things that happen before our eyes, for which marriage and worldly life become the cause.
Go to the court, read the laws written concerning such matters, and there you will see the affairs of marriage.
For when you hear physicians speaking about the wretchedness of various diseases, you understand the wretchedness of these human bodies;

in the same way, when you read the laws and see the punishments for the many kinds of evil, you will come to know the affairs of the world and the calamities of marriage, when you read of its many kinds of lawlessness.
For just as a physician does not speak of the cure of diseases that do not exist, so neither does the law introduce punishment for evils that do not exist.
Chapter
But why is it necessary to speak in so paltry a way of the evils of such a life, and to demonstrate its calamities only by adulteries, murders, and deaths?
For this is what I think: that all the wickedness of this world,
which is found in many forms in all the affairs of the world, finds no place among people who have truly separated themselves from the world and from that vain life.
And understand this statement of ours in this way, that it is true. For whoever sees the deception of this world with the purified eye of the soul, rises above its affairs, and, as the Apostle says,

[Whoever] counts all of the world's good as stench and wretchedness and makes himself a stranger to it has no share at all in those human evils — I mean covetousness and envy, anger, love of vainglory, and all the others that belong to such affairs.

And when he holds all such things in contempt and his life is entirely free and peaceful, he no longer has dispute or envy over anything, since he is no longer a lover of the things from which envy is born.
For the one whose life has been raised above the whole world, and who has counted virtue alone as his own precious possession, has a life that is always untroubled, undistressed, and peaceful.
For the possession of virtue, even though all people may receive of it, fills each one according to his capacity, and it remains undiminished; it is not like earthly possessions,
which people divide up in various ways, and however much they add to one portion, by so much they diminish another, and because of this there are battles and envy over the greater share.

But that possession is free of envy, and greed for it brings no disturbance, and the one who seizes more of it causes no hardship to anyone who wishes to acquire as much as he has; rather, as much as anyone can hold,
he himself is filled with that good desire, and that wealth of virtues is not diminished for others.
And so, whoever looks toward such a life as this and stores up for himself virtue, which no human boundary circumscribes, would he consent to incline his soul toward any low and vile things?
Or would he ever marvel at earthly wealth, or human power, or anything else that appears marvelous to foolish people?
For if anyone is still brought low among such things and loves such things that are nothing, he is outside the company of the true strivers and has no share in this discourse of ours.
But if he contemplates heavenly things and dwells with God in his mind, he is higher than all this, since he does not have the cause of such error, by which I mean marriage.

For that evil passion of pride — and if anyone called it the seed or root of all the thorns of sin, he would not stray from the truth — that passion takes the occasion of its beginning chiefly from marriage.

And likewise the evil of greed begins from it, for every married person brings forward his children as an excuse for greed, and every arrogant person boasts of the glory of his kin and strives not to become in any way inferior to those who were before him.

And likewise the other passions that are sicknesses of the soul, envy and the remembering of wrongs, hatred and others like them, arise from this same cause. For all these are found among those who love the affairs of the world.

The one who has become a stranger to these people and has gone out from among them, as if he had climbed up to some high lookout, sees human passions from afar and pities the wretchedness of those who are enslaved to such vanity and who set great value on the pleasure of the flesh.
For when such a person sees someone among men who is glorious and adorned with honor, wealth and power,
He laughs at the folly of those who boast of such things, and he counts up the longest span of human life, as the Psalmist says,

and he compares its length with the ages of eternal life, and understands how worthless and nothing this transient world is, together with everything in it. And when he understands this, he then pities the wretchedness of those who boast and rejoice so much over this nothing.
For what among the things of this world is worthy of being called blessed? Consider: among men, honor and glory from many people are desired more than anything.
What profit, then, is added to anyone from this, since the mortal remains mortal, whether he is honored or not?
Or will you say that an abundance of possessions is good? But understand what its gain is, other than this: that the fool imagines to be his what is not his, for the wretch is without understanding
that "the earth is truly the Lord's, and its fullness,"
for "God is the King of all the earth." But the passion of human greed falsely gives the name of lordship over what is not theirs,
For "the earth," as the wise Solomon says in Ecclesiastes, "abides forever," and it serves all generations and nourishes each of those who come upon it in turn.
But men, who have no authority even over their own selves, but are subject to the will of the One who holds them, when they do not know it,

They enter this life and then, even when they do not wish it, depart from it again. Yet in their great vanity they imagine that they, who are born and die from one time to the next, are lords of this ever-abiding world.

But he who understands all this, and who therefore holds in contempt every affair of the world that people count as honorable, and who has love only for that divine life, who knows that "all flesh is grass and all the glory of man is as the flower of grass": when would such a one ever regard as desirable the "grass"
that exists today and tomorrow comes to nothing? For the truly understanding person knows that not only do human affairs have no firmness,
but that neither does the whole world abide without end. Therefore he regards this temporal life as foreign and passing away.
For according to the word of the Savior, "heaven and earth will pass away", and all material things will be changed. And for this reason, as long as such a person is still "in this flesh",
this vain life seems heavy to him, and he laments that this sojourn is prolonged, as the Psalmist does in his songs.
For truly "those who have become sojourners" are in darkness among these evils.
For this reason the prophet sighed over the prolonging of his sojourn and said, "Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged," and he gave that dwelling place the name "darkness," and said:
"And I dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar", for in the Hebrew language "darkness" is called "Kedar", as we have learned from the wise. Or is it not so?

Truly, as if seized by utter darkness, people are so blind that they cannot recognize the deception of the world. They do not know that whatever in this life is reckoned good or evil by people is so only by the supposition of the senseless.
For in and of themselves they are nothing,

for neither being the child of the poor is anything, nor being the child of the rich; neither glory and wealth are anything, nor power, nor poverty and weakness; neither lordship over others is anything, nor slavery, nor any other disorder of this world. Yet among these things there is a great difference in the eyes of the foolish, who have made fleshly desire the judge of such matters.

But he whose mind has reached the divine height sees all these things as equal, and none of such matters seems to him more honorable than another, because in repose and in hardship, in wealth and in poverty,

in slavery and in lordship, the course of our life runs alike, and both have equal power with respect to the end, whether of living well or of living ill, as the apostle says: "with weapons of the right hand and of the left, through glory and dishonor."

For in both of these lives the understanding and careful person walks his road alike and hastens to reach his end. He neither takes delight in restful circumstances nor is brought low by harsh ones, but, after the custom of travelers, he goes straight ahead and pays no great attention to the things he sees. For travelers have this custom:

As they go on their way, whether they pass by gardens and flowery places or rocky and thorny ones, the good places do not hold them back with their beauty, nor do the hard places discourage them with their ugliness. Rather, because they are hurrying toward their lodging, they pass by everything alike.

Likewise the God-fearing person, who longs for eternal life, hastens without stopping toward the true dwelling that lies ahead of him. He pays attention to nothing visible along the way, but keeps his eyes lifted to heaven alone and crosses the sea of this world,
just as a good helmsman steers his ship calmly into harbor.
But the coarse person, bent down in mind and soul toward the desires of the flesh, is like a beast turned toward its pasture, turned only to the life of the belly and the passions born of the belly,
both "estranged from the divine life" and "separated from the eternal promises,"

and nothing seems good to him except the pleasures of the flesh. Such a person and everyone like him "walks in darkness," as Scripture says. For among such people dwell greed and a love of defilement, immoderate in its desires,
love of power and the craving for empty glory, and the other hosts of passions that enter into people.
For among evils, one follows another, and when one has settled in someone, the others also come to him, as if drawn by some natural compulsion,

just as, if someone takes hold of one end of a chain and pulls it, it is impossible for all the links hanging from one another not to follow. Instead, the one part of the first bent link draws the part of the second bent link attached to it, and that link in turn draws the one after it, and that one another, until the links attached to one another come to an end.
In the same way the passions are attached and joined to one another, and through the one that enters first, the other ranks of evils settle in the soul.
And if you wish to picture that evil chain, consider
how someone might be overcome by some desire through vainglory,

and along with vainglory comes the desire for possessions as well, for no one becomes covetous unless vainglory leads him to it. Then the passion of covetousness kindles in him anger toward his fellows, arrogance toward those beneath him, and envy toward those above him.
Envy is followed by duplicity, duplicity by bitterness, and bitterness by hatred of mankind, and the end of all this is judgment and being handed over to Gehenna, to the outer darkness, and to fire.

Again, negligence arises through slackness of mind, and slackness is followed by gluttony and sleep. From these comes blindness of mind, from blindness of mind fornication, from that despair, and from despair the descent into Gehenna. Likewise vainglory is followed by pride, as we also said above, pride by judging one's neighbor, and judging by God's abandonment of the person, and then come all the evils: blasphemy, fornication, and every wickedness, and then the descent into hell, as he deserves. Do you see this rank of evils, how they all follow one another?

And since this rank of evils has once entered this world, we find, as we have gathered from the holy Scriptures, one deliverance from them: that a person should separate himself from such a life, which has this host of passions joined to it.
For it is impossible, while remaining in the city of Sodom, to escape that rain of fire. And it is impossible,
If anyone went out of Sodom and turned back again to look at its destruction, would he not become a pillar of salt? Nor can anyone be freed from slavery to the Egyptians who does not leave Egypt,
– I mean the dark and gloomy life of the world – and let him cross not the Red Sea, but this black and dark sea of this vain life.

And if, as the Lord says, unless "the truth sets us free," we remain in that evil slavery, how is it possible for someone to enter into the truth who seeks falsehood and "lives in the error of the world"?
Or how can anyone be saved from this slavery who has willingly cast his own life into slavery and bound himself with its bonds?
And if you wish, let us illustrate our words with a parable. For just as a river in the days of winter, greatly stirred up and muddied and rushing violently, carrying along huge stones and logs,

is bitter and deadly for those who have gone down into it, but for those who stand far from it, it roars idly and in vain and does them no harm, so too the billows of the world overwhelm those who are in it, and upon them come the surges of the passions,

which swirl about in this world, and those who are found among them they submerge in their whirlpool. But if someone leaves this torrent and "these restless waters," as Scripture says, he will escape becoming prey to the teeth of the world, and like a sparrow, on the wing of virtue, he will escape the snare of the demons. 7. For, as I said in the image of the torrent,

so human life is stirred up by every kind of turmoil and disorder and always flows downward, and nothing in its affairs is firm, nor does it wait to satisfy those who desire it; rather, everything of it that comes draws near to those who seek it and at once flees with a swift current and vanishes from sight. Therefore it is good
that we put ourselves far from such a fierce torrent,

but because the man himself has drawn the covering of the eyelids over his eyes and made it a dividing wall between himself and the sun,

for the power of sight is idle when the eyes are closed and cannot do its proper work; and for this reason its idleness becomes for him the cause of darkness, brought upon himself by that man of his own will.
Or if someone builds himself a house and leaves no entrance at all for the light, he likewise remains in darkness, because he has willingly shut the door against the radiance.
So too did "the first man" act, or rather he who begot wickedness among men,

for in his nature he had the good lying before him on every side, but willingly he brought upon himself what is foreign to nature, and by turning away from virtue he created, by his own will, the experience of evil in his own mind.
For evil, apart from the will and seen in its own essence, is nothing among the things that exist, for "every creature of God is good and nothing is evil." But in this manner, as we have said,

sin entered into the life of men, and from that small cause wickedness grew and spread beyond measure among men; and that divinely lovely beauty of the soul, made in the likeness of the firstborn beauty, like a piece of iron,
was thus blackened by the venom of wickedness, and no longer had the grace of its own natural image,
but clothed itself in the squalor of sin, and the "great and honored living creature" was called mortal, when it fell from its honor, as happens to those
who stumble and fall into stinking mire and spoil their own color with that clay and become unrecognizable to those who know them,

In the same way he fell into the mire of sin, lost the likeness of the incorruptible God, and through sin put on the corruptible image of clay. But the great goodness of God did not tolerate our perdition. Instead the only-begotten Son and Word, consubstantial with the Father and sharing his throne, came down from heaven and put on this poor flesh of ours, and became like us in every respect except sin. He suffered for us and died, and raised those forgotten in hell. He became the firstborn of those who have fallen asleep, loosed the pangs of death, clothed us with that former glory, and gave us power so that, if we wish, we may be able to gain that former glory and even one far greater.
And now it is up to us, if we wish, to wash off again, as if with water, by good conduct, the mire that we have brought upon ourselves through sins after holy baptism,
so that the earthy covering may be stripped from us and the beauty of the soul may appear again.
Now stripping off what is alien is a return to what is natural, and this cannot be attained in any other way than by our becoming as we were created in the beginning.
For likeness to God is not our doing, nor a thing within human power; rather, it is the gift of God, the generous giver,
who at that first creation at once bestowed likeness to himself upon our nature. And again, when we had fallen through disobedience, he renewed us by his own coming.
But now it is our task to cleanse away the filth that has come upon us through sins and to reveal the hidden beauty of the soul.
And the Lord signifies this in the Gospel when he says, "The kingdom of heaven is within you," so that all who are able to hear the wisdom spoken in mystery may understand this.
For as I suppose, my discourse signifies this: that the goodness of God is not far from our nature, nor hard to find for those who seek it, but is always with each person;
and it is unknown and hidden when it is "choked by the desires of the world," but it is found again when we turn our mind toward it.
And if you wish us to make our discourse credible from another side as well, I think that the Lord signifies this same thing by the search for the "lost drachma,"

namely that there is no profit from the other virtues, which the text has called "drachmas," even if all of them are present, when that widowed soul lacks the one thing, which is the beauty of its own nature.
For this reason he first commands that a lamp be lit. By this, as I think, he signifies the word, which brings hidden things to light. Then, in her own house, that is,
within oneself, he says to search for the lost drachma. And by the drachma that is sought he surely signifies the image of the King,

which is not completely lost but lies hidden beneath dirt and dung. And by dirt and dung we should understand the passions of the flesh and the mire; when this is cleansed and cleared away by good living,
then what is sought will be found, and the soul itself that found it will rejoice over it and will gather its neighbors to share its joy.
For truly all those powers that dwell together with the soul, which he has now named "neighbors,"
when this great image of the King appears and shines forth, the image that was stamped from the beginning upon this drachma of ours by him who "alone fashioned our hearts,"
then they too come to that divine joy and gladness and behold the ineffable beauty of the image that has been found, for it says, "Rejoice with me,
for I have found the drachma that I had lost."
Now those neighbors and powers dwelling together with the soul, who rejoice over the finding of that divine drachma, are these:
the power of reasoning and of desire, of grief and of anger, and whatever other powers there are with the soul are rightly called "neighbors" and "friends,"
all of whom will then "rejoice in the Lord," when all of them look toward the good and all of them hasten to the glory of God and no longer become instruments of sin.
And since the means of finding what is sought, that divine image, is this: a return to that first beauty,
which is now hidden in the filth of the passions, therefore it is fitting for us to become such as the first-created man was in that first life, when he was not under the dominion of sin.
Consider what he was like. He was naked of those garments of dead skin. He looked boldly upon the face of God, and he did not judge what was good by taste and by the eye,
but "delighted in the Lord," and used the helper he had been given as a helper toward this, as Scripture says. For he had not yet known her
until he was cast out of paradise, and until she was sentenced to the torment of pains for the sin she had committed.
And now, by the same thing through which we were cast out of paradise, we must return to that same first blessedness. What, then, was the cause of our being cast out?
It was desire, entering at that time through deception, that made the beginning of the fall,

that is, the tasting of the tree. And then shame and fear followed upon that passion of desire, and no longer daring to stand before the eyes of the Creator, but hiding under leaves and shadows; and after this they covered themselves with the skin of the dead, and so they were sent into exile in this sickly world, full of scorching heat and hardship, in which marriage was devised as a consolation for dying and as a means by which humankind might not die out.

but rather the commandment of God. And this is: to touch only what is good, and not to look upon the taste of evil,

For this is why it was commanded to those first-created that they should not have "knowledge of evil along with good,"
but that they should keep away from that good which is known together with evil, and should possess the good purely and unmixed with evil,

which is nothing else, as my reasoning supposes, than to be with God alone, and to hold this as an everlasting and unceasing delight, and not to mix with that delight in the good any desire for evil as well. And if it is permitted to be bold and say it, I say this: that, as I suppose, in this way a person is caught up out of this world, which "lies in evil", and is snatched away into paradise,
where the apostle Paul went, and heard and saw things not heard and not seen, which it is not permitted for human beings to speak.

But since paradise "is the dwelling of the living" and does not receive those who have died through sin, while we are fleshly and mortal, sold under sin, how is it possible to enter "that land of the living"
for one who is held fast by the tyranny of death?
Or what means might anyone find to be set free from this power? But the teaching of the Gospel is sufficient for this too.
For we have heard in the Gospel how the Lord said to Nicodemus:
"What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit."
And we know that the flesh is condemned to death because of sin, but the Spirit of God is incorruptible, life-giving and immortal.
And just as along with fleshly birth there is also implanted the power of death [?], which destroys the one who is born,
so also the Spirit implants the life-giving power in those born of it. And what is revealed to us by these words?
Only this: that we should withdraw from the fleshly life, which death follows without doubt, and should complete such a life as no longer drags along the chain of death.
And this is the life of virginity and monasticism. And that these things are said truthfully I will show briefly.
For who would not know this, that the fleshly union of marriage has as its work the making of mortal bodies,
And, as I said, this is the task set before such a person; but in the communion of the Spirit, life and incorruption are begotten, in place of children, for those who have shared in it,

"and through that childbearing is saved" the spiritual mother of such children, with joy, as the Psalmist said in the divine songs: "He settles the barren woman in a house joyfully, as a mother rejoicing over children."
For truly the virgin soul rejoices, which bears those immortal children through the Holy Spirit, and which, because of its purity and virginity, has been called barren by the prophet.

Now therefore, let such a life be honored by all who have understanding, for it is above the power of death.

For bodily childbearing (let no one find this statement strange) becomes for people a cause not of life but rather of death. For corruption has its beginning from birth; and those who have separated themselves from it through virginity or the monastic life

have halted within themselves the course of death and have not let it go forward through them; they have made themselves like a dividing wall between death and life, and have not allowed death to run any further through them.
And since death cannot pass beyond virginity, but comes up to it and is undone, it is clearly shown that virginity is above the power of death.
And rightly is that body called incorrupt which does not serve in the service of the life of corruption, nor undertakes to become an instrument of mortal generation.
For by this the union of corruption and dying has been cut off. Therefore, from Adam until the days of the Virgin, death was not cut off,

for it was impossible for death to be idle, since the birth of people came about through marriage. Rather, it went along with all the first generations, and from time to time it entered together with those who were entering this life.
And virginity was found to be the limit of its power and what holds it back, and it is impossible for death to pass beyond it.
For just as happened in the case of Mary the Mother of God, that "death" which "reigned from Adam" until her,
when it came to her and encountered the fruit of virginity, was at once shattered, so also with every soul
that completes in virginity the life of the time of its being in this flesh, the power of death is shattered and undone, when it has no one in whom to fix its sting.
For fire too, if wood and reed and hay are not added to it,

or something else that kindles it, cannot blaze up of itself. So neither can the power of death find the means to spread, unless marriage gives it material and brings mortals into the world and prepares them for it.
And if you are in doubt about these words, read through the names of those trials which come upon people through death,

how many they are, as we said at the very beginning of the discourse, and understand where their beginning comes from: from virginity or from marriage. Or is the mourning of widowhood or of orphanhood possible, or being torn apart in trials over children, unless marriage first comes in, which is the parent of all this?
For the joys and gladness and desires and pleasures that are in marriage go along with all these pains.
For just as a sword is smooth to the touch, and bright and clean and pleasing to the will, but its edge is an instrument of death,
terrible to see and more terrible to the one it strikes, such also is marriage: it appears like something finely polished to the touch and restful to the bodily senses,
But when it comes into the hands of the one who has laid hold of it, it brings in along with itself the arrival of sorrows as well, for it is the cause of mourning and trials for people.
This brings to view pitiable sights, full of tears:

children orphaned in the time of infancy, lying exposed to be seized by the powerful, who often smile in the midst of that very trial out of ignorance of their misfortunes. And what else brings about widowhood? Is it not marriage?
Therefore separation from it dispels all these evils that come unforeseen. And this matter is not strange.
For where the judgment laid from the beginning on those who sinned is dissolved, and no longer is the sorrow of women,
according to the word of Scripture, multiplied, and sorrow no longer goes before the birth of human beings, it is evident
that along with it the trial of this world is dissolved too, and the tear is wiped from the eyes, as the prophet says,
when there is no longer "conception in iniquity, nor birth in sin," nor birth from blood, nor by the will of the flesh, nor by the will of man, but birth comes about from God.
And this happens when a person conceives in the living place of his heart the incorruption of the Spirit and gives birth to "wisdom and righteousness,
holiness and redemption." For it is possible for everyone who wishes to be a mother of him who is the wisdom of God, righteousness and holiness and redemption, as the Lord himself says:
"Whoever does my will, he is my brother and sister and mother." What place, then, would death find among such offspring?
Truly, "among them death has been swallowed up in victory by life," and so I think that the way of life of virginity and monasticism is an image of "that eternal life" and blessedness.

For many hold within themselves images of the good things that lie ahead in hope; and if anyone investigates, he will find the truth of my words in this way. First, when "a person dies to sin, he lives to God" and no longer bears "the fruit of death": the one who has separated himself from marriage and from the world and has put on the form of the ascetics' way of struggle, and, as far as his strength allows,
has brought about an end of bodily life,

and from then on awaits "the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ," and no longer makes any partition between himself and the coming of Christ through the generations of kin that would be brought in by him through marriage.
And then, beyond this, he gains in this very life the greatest of all the good things that are to be revealed at the resurrection.

For since the life of the righteous is then to be made like that of the angels, according to the Lord's promise, and one characteristic of the angelic nature is to be a stranger to marriage, to vain cares and to fleshly desires, and those who practice true monasticism have this same thing, in this way such a person has in some manner already obtained that good thing of the resurrection,
joined to "the brightness of the saints," and made like the purity of the bodiless beings by the undefiled and carefree character of his life.
And since virginity and monasticism are the bringers of such things, what word could worthily praise that grace?
Or what other thing so great and honorable could be found that it could be made equal to its greatness?

so that it may not become one flesh with it, nor accept anything else among the things opposed to life. For defilement is common to all the passions, and if the soul is defiled by any one of them, it can no longer possess its spotless garment.
And it is good also to illustrate this word by a comparison: for just as the water in a lake, so long as nothing has fallen into it, stays calm and clean,
but if a stone falls in, the lake and its calm are broken up, for the stone cuts through the water and goes down into the depth,
and from it a wave arises, and waters rise up upon waters, and the wave goes out from the middle to the edge, and the lake is filled with waves,
so likewise the calm and quiet of the soul is wholly troubled when some one passion falls into it and stirs it up.
And those who truly have knowledge of virtue say this also: that it is impossible for someone to acquire one virtue fittingly and well without the others also coming along with it,
but with whomever even one virtue has settled, the others also follow along with him without doubt.
Now then, it is likewise with the opposite as well, for whichever power of our soul is harmed, all the rest follow it. And truly, as the Apostle says, all share in that one member.
And if one member suffers, all grieve with it, and if one is glorified, all rejoice with it.

For in this way Israel crossed the sea under the leadership of Moses, and the Egyptian went up onto that road and was drowned, each one because of the mind that was in him; for Israel went lightly over it,
But the Egyptian went down into the deep. In the same way, then, virtue is a light thing that rises upward,
for all who practise it "fly like clouds," according to the word of Isaiah the prophet, and "like doves with their young." But sin is heavy and sits on a talent of lead,
according to the word of the prophet; for, as the Apostle says, "These things happened to them as a type, and were written for our instruction."
[?] And the prophetess Miriam too gives us to understand this same thing,

who, when they had crossed the sea, took up a timbrel and led the assembly of women. For, as I think, by the timbrel the text signifies virginity, first taken up by Miriam, who, I think, foreshadows Mary the Mother of God.
For just as a timbrel is made from the skin of a dead animal and gives out a loud sound,
so virginity becomes exalted and renowned when it has within itself no share in this worldly life.
And since the timbrel that Miriam held was dead, and the deadness of the flesh is virginity, this is by no means unfitting,
that the prophetess was a virgin. For this may be supposed by us, although we do not know it for certain, that the prophetess Miriam became the leader of the company of virgins,
since many say of her that she was unmarried, for nowhere does it mention in detail her marriage or her bearing of children,
since otherwise she would have been named not after Aaron and Moses but after a husband, for the head of a woman is her husband.
For if virginity appears among those for whom childbearing was honorable and blessed and sought after,
should we not all the more eagerly acquire it, we who hear the word of Scripture not in a carnal but in a spiritual way?!
For we hear from Scripture that childbearing is good, but let us understand of what the pursuit of childbearing in the Old Testament was a figure.

For the prophet Isaiah and the apostle Paul make known to us what kind of childbearing befits the saints. The one said, "Through fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and were in labor and gave birth to the spirit of your salvation"; and Paul, who strove
to become rich in children, to the point that he bore cities and nations, and not only brought Corinthians and Galatians to the light by his own womb through the Lord,
but "from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum" he filled the world with his own children,
"whom he begot in Christ through the Gospel." Blessed also is the womb of virginity, which served that incorruptible birth,
and neither did the birth undo the virginity, nor did the virginity become destructive of such a birth, for where "the spirit of salvation is born,"
as Isaiah says, there all the passions of the flesh become useless.

And we have heard from the apostle this saying as well: each human being is twofold. One is the visible one, whose nature is to be given over to corruption. The other is in the hidden places of the heart, and it receives renewal.

And since a human being is twofold, it is not unreasonable for us to understand marriage as twofold as well: one marriage of the outer person and one of the inner. Whoever says that purity of the flesh helps that inner marriage says nothing that departs from the truth. 2. And just as it is impossible

for a person to set out to practise two crafts at once with his own hands, such as farming and ploughing with oxen while at the same time sailing on the sea, or working as a smith while at the same time working as a [?], but if he wants to do one, he must give up the other,

so too, since two marriages are before us, one accomplished through the flesh and the other of the spirit, let it be known that joining oneself to one of them brings about separation from the other. For neither can the eye see two things set apart from each other at once, unless, in seeing the one, it withdraws from seeing the other, and when it looks at this one, it is cut off from seeing that one.
Nor can the tongue serve many languages at once,
so as to speak both Hebrew and Greek together. Nor can the ear listen at once to tales and to words of instruction,
for the distinction of the sound, if each is heard separately,
...enters the mind of the hearer; but if they are mixed together and heard in that way, the mind is no longer able to separate them from one another.
In the same way, then, the power of desire implanted in us cannot both serve fleshly desires and bring about the spiritual marriage,
for the two are not acquired by one and the same activity,
but fasting, the mortification of the flesh and contempt for all fleshly things become the guide to the spiritual marriage, while everything opposite to these becomes the helper of fleshly desire.
And just as, if there were two lords to choose between, so that a person might submit to one of them, since it is impossible to serve "two lords" at once,

whoever is sensible would choose the one from whom the greater benefit comes; so too, since two marriages lie before us and it is impossible to be in both, for "the unmarried man cares for the things of the Lord and the married man cares for the things of the world."
This is the task of wise people: that we not be cut off from choosing what is better, and that we not remain ignorant of the way that leads to the Lord, which is found in the following manner.
for just as in fleshly marriage, the one who strives to become desirable and beloved to all works hard at it,
so as to be delicate in body and adorned with clothing, and so that not from his way of life either, [?]
nor from his lineage should any reproach fall upon him,
so too whoever longs for that spiritual marriage must first show himself renewed and removed from all oldness by the renewal of the mind,
and then become rich, not with the treasures of the earth, but with the treasures of heaven.

And as for nobility of birth, let it not be this vain kind that comes of its own accord, which many wicked people also have, but that which has been acquired by labor and zeal through one's own virtues,
which only those have who are sons of light and children of God and "a noble race from the rising of the sun," on account of the honor and brightness of their deeds.
And let him acquire well-being, not by fattening his flesh, but by the very opposite, so that through weakness of the flesh he may bring to perfection the power of the spirit.
And I know also the dowry of this marriage, made not from corruptible riches, but given by the Spirit from one's own wealth. Do you wish to learn the names of those riches?
Listen to Paul, the steward of that good marriage; these are those riches:
first of all holiness, righteousness, peace, joy and things like these, the fruits of the Spirit which he enumerates; all such things are the gifts of that marriage.

And listen again also to Solomon, how he says that we should bring in true wisdom as a companion to dwell with us, concerning whom he cries out: "Love her passionately, that she may guard you; honor her, that she may embrace you."
For by these words he urges every person to acquire the garment worthy of that marriage and in this way to celebrate the feast at that wedding with those who rejoice,
so that he may not be thrown outside when he begs to share in that festival
while not wearing the wedding garment. And it is clear that this saying applies alike to men and women, young and old, for, as the Apostle says,
"There is neither male nor female, but Christ is all in all."
And since this is so, whoever has become a lover of wisdom has that divine desire and longing, which is true wisdom,
and the soul that is joined to the incorruptible Bridegroom has the love of true wisdom, which is God.
But what that spiritual marriage is, and toward what face that holy and heavenly love looks, has been made clear to us by these few things that have been said.

However, since drawing near to the purity of God without a like purity that befits it
is impossible, therefore we are obliged to build a high and firm dividing wall between ourselves and the desires of the flesh,
so that the purity of the soul may not be defiled by their approach. And the firm dividing wall is hatred of and separation from all passionate things,
for desire is one in nature, and just as water from one spring flows into many channels, so it spreads out over all the senses and, according to each sense, mingles with those who love pleasure.
and from whatever perceptible thing a person takes in desire,
by that same thing his heart has been wounded, as the Lord teaches us: whoever fulfils the desire of the eyes has received the passion of that sin into his heart.
For I think that by that one sense, the eyes, the Lord signified all the senses, so that we might follow his word.
And we may rightly add this as well: that whoever hears something with desire, or touches something with desire, or bends any other of the powers within us toward desire, has sinned in his heart.
But so that this may not happen, the monk who wishes to live in purity must make it a rule in his life to love nothing in which the forge [?] of desire is hidden, and,
first of all, to guard himself against the desire for foods, for it is like the mother of battles; and when desires for foods and drinks multiply,
they fill the flesh with that fullness of evils from which multitudes of passions are born.
And therefore, so that our body may be at peace and not be stirred up by a surfeit of passions, we must
strive for fasting and not make desire the measure and limit of eating, but rather the need for each thing,
and even though there is desire in the taking of what is needed, for want knows how to make everything sweet and to be taken with desire, what is needed is not evil because of that desire,
but we ought to choose out what is good from everything and to despise the ease of the flesh.
For we also see how farmers separate wheat from chaff, so that they may use each in its proper place: wheat as food for people, and chaff for burning or as feed for cattle.

In the same way, let the laborer of purity separate what is needed from desire, like wheat from chaff, and let him cast the harmful part to the beastly ones, whose end is burning, as the Apostle says,
and let him depart from them, and let him receive with thanksgiving what his own nature needs.

But many have swerved to the other side of immoderation and gone astray through excessive fasting. They have cut their souls off from the lofty contemplations, and their mind no longer moved in freedom,

but turned back to the flesh itself. Therefore it is good to guard against this as well and to keep far from immoderation on both sides. Then we will neither darken our mind through gluttony nor, on the other hand, bring diseases upon our bodies and so bring the mind low by turning it toward the weakness of the flesh,

but let us remember that word of wisdom which condemns equally any swerving to the right side or to the left. For our body is compounded of four elements, not alike but opposed to one another: hot and cold, moist and dry. The hot is blended with the cold, and the moist with the dry, beyond what words can describe,
for they are united by natures that come in between them.
And so those elements, separated from one another, are blended by means of foods, and the cold and the hot are blended by means of moist and dry foods.
And again, the moist and the dry are united by means of cold and hot things. And so, from foods distinct from one another, the unity of those opposites comes about.
And why should I speak at length about how they are separated and united, as God wills?
For I have brought this in here so that we too may maintain their balance and not increase the one and diminish the other,
but may imitate the one who stands on the chariot.
For just as, if the horses are not running evenly, he does not do this: strike the swift runner so that it goes still faster, nor does he stifle the sluggish and slow one with the bridle,
nor does he leave free the one that is hard to turn and pulls away, so that it may run in disorder wherever it wishes,
but he straightens the one that is hard to turn, and the one that pulls away he checks [?], and he hurries the slow ones, until he makes them all even in their running,

so too must our mind, which is the one standing over the flesh and holding its reins, act: so that neither, when heat is excessive in the time of youth, should it procure things that increase the heat, nor, when coldness has increased because of illnesses or old age, should it foster that coldness by taking cooling foods.
And in every other matter let it do this, "so that neither the excess may increase nor the deficiency be diminished,"

but let it do away with immoderation on both sides, and let it make the flesh neither disorderly aroused and unbridled through gluttony and luxury, nor sick and weak and slack for ascetic struggle through excessive fasting.
This is the perfect rule of fasting: that a person should not look to the concerns of the flesh,
but to carrying out the services of the soul, so that only its own purity and spiritual struggle may not be ruined, whether by eating or by excessive fasting.

As for how each deed that belongs to this life ought to be done, and how mercy is needed, for anyone who wishes to learn well
there are also writings that teach about such matters,
yet seeing in deed is truer than learning by word, and there is no difficulty at all in the matter,
that one should have to find that teacher by traveling distant roads and seas; rather, "the word is near," as the Apostle says, and here is the teaching of virtue,
where such a life as this has truly been brought to success, and the heavenly way of life is taught both by deed and by word. For every word without deeds, even if it is adorned,
is like a lifeless image that looks beautiful because of the colors of its pigments,
but he who both does and teaches, as the Gospel says, is truly a living man and a doer of deeds of beautiful goodness.

Therefore, then, whoever takes up the monastic life and the way of life of virginity must find such a leader. For just as a man cannot learn some foreign language by himself, even if he greatly desires to learn it,
but learns it from those who know it, and only in this way becomes able to converse in those foreign tongues,
so it is with this life also. Since we have made our nature a stranger to the works of virtue and ignorant of them through our evil way of life,

it is now impossible to learn it in any other way than under the guidance of one in whom it has been brought to success. For all the crafts of this world are advanced through the instruction of those who know them, and no one becomes a smith, or a carpenter, or anything else by himself. And since the things of the world happen in this way, what then shall we say about this matter?

For this is not a new and recently begun matter, such that out of helplessness we should entrust to ourselves the finding of what is better; nor is it a bodily matter, such that if we failed to find what is better, it would do us no harm.

But just as the art of medicine, which at first was unknown, was discovered by men through the Lord's gift, and they came to recognize both what is beneficial and what is harmful through experience, and in this way established that practice,
and now whoever wishes to learn that art
has no hardship of testing drugs by himself to find which ones cleanse the body and which ones are deadly, but learns what was discovered by others and in this way succeeds in that art,
and likewise about this spiritual healing, which is virtue, by which we heal all the passions of the soul.

What hardship is there, that we should have to acquire it by our own reflection and toil? Rather, it is easy to learn from someone who has been guided on the right path by much teaching from others and by long experience.
For ignorance and youth are a stumbling block in every matter, and no one will find that any good thing has anywhere succeeded without experience and knowledge.
And the more this matter surpasses every other matter, the greater the caution we need concerning it, so that we may not go astray in it.
For in those other matters, if an error occurs, perhaps there may be a loss of money and a fall from bodily honor,
but in this great and lofty matter the loss is not one of money, nor of worldly and passing glory,
nor of anything else that comes to us from outside; rather, the damage of the error touches the soul itself, and its perdition is the result.
For whoever loses an inherited possession is not without hope of recovering his former wealth by some means; but whoever loses his own soul, how shall he find it?
And since many who enter this life are ignorant and inexperienced, let this be their remedy:
that first of all they find a guide on this road and a good teacher, so that they may not, through their ignorance, stray into pathless and thorny places.
For "two are better than one," as Solomon says, and the one, when he is ignorant, is easily brought down by the enemy, who lies in wait for every person.

And truly, "woe to such a one," according to the word of the same wise Solomon, for "when he falls, he has no one to raise him up." For this is what happened to certain people who with good intention put on this honorable habit, but as soon as they entered into it, they immediately set about reaching for the measure of perfection; and having risen from that one fall, they fell by another fall, that of haughtiness, for by the error of their minds they deceived themselves and reckoned as good whatever their minds inclined toward.
These are the ones whom Wisdom has named "idle," who have strewn thorns upon their own paths, who have abandoned the apostolic teachings and have taken up idleness as their work.

From among these come the dreamers, who trust the delusions of dreams more than the words of the Gospel and call demonic fantasies appearances of angels. And there are others again who have counted brutishness, harshness and hatred of people as virtue, knowing nothing of the fruit of solitude and humility.

And how could anyone recount all such falls, and how many evils lack of discernment and following one's own will lead to? For from this cause we know of certain people who persisted in hunger until death, thinking, "Such a fast is pleasing to God."

And still others, by following their own wills, have swerved to the other side. They have taken on monasticism and celibacy in name only and have become no better in any way than laypeople, not only because they have handed their belly over to the craving for foods,

but they even lived in the world and openly kept company with women, and they called such mingling with them harmless, so as to cover the evil suspicion about them with the name of passionlessness; and they made this lofty work appear contemptible.

Therefore it is right that those newly come out of the world should not lay down a law for themselves, for this life of ours does not lack good guides; rather, this way of life now shines brightly among us and flourishes,
and those can find it who walk in that good track, follow the fragrance of that ointment, and "are filled with the fragrance of Christ."
For just as a lamp, when lit, gives light to all who follow it and itself loses none of its light by giving light to others,

so too the holiness of this way of life spreads from its leader to the others who follow him. For true is that word of the prophet: "He who is with the holy, the spotless and the chosen becomes such as well."
If, then, you are looking for a sign, so that you do not go wrong in finding such a guide, his sign is clear:
If, then, you see a man whose way of life stands between death and life, who chooses the better course on both sides and does not have the inactivity of death in keeping the commandments,
nor again is alive to the desires of the world, but wherever a matter of the flesh appears, there he is more unmoved than the dead,
yet toward the works of virtue, by which those who are truly spiritual are made known, he is truly strong and courageous and vigorous.
Look to such a rule of life; let it be for you the model of the divine life.

Imitate his old age and his youth as well, and rather imitate the old age in his youth and the youth in his old age, for neither did old age dissolve his courage and the vigor of his years, nor was his youth a worker of folly,
but there was a kind of union of opposites in both, or rather an exchange of nature,
for in old age the strength for what is good was young, and in youth that time of life was idle toward evil.
And if you inquire about his desires, imitate that strong and ardent love of divine wisdom which remained with him from youth until old age.
But if you are unable to look at him, as those with weak eyes cannot look at the sun, go to that assembly of saints appointed under him, who shine greatly,

many of whom, young in years, became elders in the works of purity, and by their understanding anticipated old age, and by their deeds outran time, and who showed their love of wisdom to be fiercer and mightier than bodily loves, not because their natures were any different, for in all people "the flesh has war against the spirit," but for this reason:
because they listened well to the one who speaks, saying that purity "is a tree of life to all who take hold of it." Seated on this wood, as on a well-made raft, the waves of youth
they passed through, and they reached the harbor of God's will;
and now their blessed souls are in calm and in fair, waveless weather, because of their good crossing from this world,
they who anchored their conduct on that good hope, as a ship is held by strong anchors, and became fearless of the waves, and,
like luminaries from the height of heaven, set out the splendors of their own deeds before all who wish to follow their goodness.
Now then, let us too, by hope in God, pass without going astray through that sea of temptation, we who have entered that angelic way of life and are guided aright in it.

Why then do you search out and count up where certain people entered this way of life and were defeated by the passions, and their undertaking came to nothing, and for this reason you are without hope, as though toward an impossible thing?

Look to those who have carried it through well, and you too take confidence and venture on that good voyage, by the ship of the Holy Spirit, under the pilotage of Christ, in the ship of purity, guided aright by God the Father. For neither
"Those who go down to the sea in ships and do business in many waters," when shipwreck has befallen some, do [not ?] make it the ruin of their own hope,
but they clothe themselves in good hope and hasten to the end of their journey.

Or is it not worse than everything else, out of this caution lest error should befall you in this holy life, to grow old in errors and sins all the days of your life and to reckon this decision the better one?
For if it is evil to draw near to sin even once, and for this reason you think it better not to approach that higher life at all,
how much worse is it to remain in sin your whole life, and for this reason to stay entirely far from that holy life?
How do you hear the words of the Crucified, you who live in desires? He died for your sins, yet you are alive in them! How do you hear his commandment, which bids us follow him and,

as a trophy of victory over the demons, carry the cross on our shoulders, when you are not crucified to the world and do not accept the putting to death of the flesh? How do you believe those words of the apostle Paul,
the one who beseeches you "to present your body as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God", you who "are conformed to this world
and are not transformed by the renewal of your mind", "nor do you walk in your new life", but still the works "of the old man"
you hold on to?! How are you a priest of God, you who were anointed for this very purpose, that you might offer gifts to him, yet gifts that are not foreign to you, nor brought in from outside,
but that which is truly yours, namely "your inner man," which must also, in order to be perfect and holy, as was said of the lamb, be separated from every blemish and disease?!
How then will you offer this to God, you who do not listen to the law, which commands that nothing unclean be offered?!

And if you desire to see God, why do you not listen to Moses, who commands the people to purify themselves from marriage and from every worldly affair, so that they may be able to receive the manifestation of God?!
But if all this seems little to you — "being crucified with Christ," "presenting oneself as a sacrifice to God,"

"being a priest of God Most High," being made worthy of that great vision of God — what shall we find for you higher than all this?! For if these things seem little to you and not great, you will surely also reckon as little the good things that come from them,
for from being crucified with him come also living with him and glory and reigning with him,
and from presenting oneself before God, the likeness of the angelic nature is granted to us in place of human nature.
And whoever has acquired true priesthood and has been joined to the great high priest, "he too shall remain a priest forever, no longer given over into the hands of death."
But what other fruit of the vision of God shall we speak of? For it has no other fruit,

except the very vision of God, for this is the head of all hope and greater than all desire, and the end and summit of all the blessings and promises of God and of those ineffable good things that surpass all knowledge,

which Moses too longed to see, and all the prophets and kings and righteous ones." But only the "pure in heart" are made worthy of it, who for this reason are truly "blessed" and are also called blessed,
"for they shall see God." It is my wish that you too may be one of them, "crucified with Christ," standing before God,
a spotless priest and offering, made holy with all the holiness of virginity, prepared for the coming of the Lord, so that you too may "see God with a pure heart,"

"according to the promise of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ," to whom belong glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and unto the ages of ages, amen! Pray for Father Euthymius, who translated this book. May God glorify him in spirit. Amen.
